title: Weapons to Russia, Wigs to China: How North Korea Balances Its Allies
gist: North Korea opened a road bridge with Russia in September and one with China last week; the author argues a division of labor, with Russia supplying military help and China economic help, keeps both alliances complementary (truncated excerpt).

insights.claim: North Korea opened its first road bridge with Russia in September and a similar bridge with China the following month.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: Physical infrastructure indicates deepening trade links with both patrons.

insights.claim: The Russia bridge will strengthen the bilateral arms trade, while the China bridge will supply energy products, raw materials and heavy equipment for domestic consumption.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: Arms-for-support with Russia and commodity flows from China sustain Pyongyang against sanctions pressure.

insights.claim: North Korea seeks military assistance from Russia and economic help from China, and this clear division of labor makes the alliances complementary rather than competitive.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: Pyongyang is unlikely to be forced to choose between patrons, reducing leverage for either to pressure it.
